title: Photography direction for a recruiting firm
metaTitle: Photography for a recruiting firm site
excerpt: Choose photographs that show the kind of role you fill. A handshake is a mood, not an argument. The picture has to survive without the headline.
alt: A glass-walled office corridor with a sofa, a floor lamp, and black pendant lights, a lobby view that does not show the kind of role a search firm fills.
caption: A corridor can be handsome and still say nothing about the seat. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should photographs on a recruiting site show?
faqs.answer: Show the kind of role you fill: the workplace, the scorecard, or the person who runs the search with that artifact. A hiring manager who has been burned is checking the picture against their own company. A lobby, a skyline, or a handshake does not answer that check.

faqs.question: When is stock photography acceptable?
faqs.answer: Use stock when it shows a workplace you actually recruit into, and say if it is a typical setting rather than a client. Do not imply you placed the person in the frame. Reject handshakes and generic meetings. Fewer true pictures are stronger than a grid of costumes.

faqs.question: How should alt text be written for these pictures?
faqs.answer: Describe what is in the frame, then the claim it supports, as if the image failed to load. Do not write a slogan or hide a keyword in the description. A screen-reader user should hear the scene. If type sits on the photo, keep the words readable.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Recruiting firm website photography should show the kind of role you fill. A handshake does not. The pictures are part of the argument, not a mood pasted under the headline. Nielsen Norman Group's page research says the first 10 seconds decide whether people stay, and many leave within 10 to 20 seconds. In those seconds the largest picture is read with the sentence beside it. If the picture is two people in suits clasping hands, the sentence about plant managers never gets a fair hearing.

Choose frames a hiring manager who has been burned before can check against their own company. A floor, a clinic desk, a scorecard, the person who will run the search sitting with that scorecard. If a frame could sit on any firm's site, it is not evidence. It is costume.

## The picture is a claim

Every photograph on the site makes a claim, whether you intended one or not. A glass lobby claims you are a downtown firm. A skyline claims you are a city. A handshake claims the work is a meeting. None of those claims answers the question this buyer brought: do you fill roles like mine.

Put the claim in a sentence before you book a photographer. "We fill plant-leadership roles in owner-operated factories." Then ask which picture would still make that sentence true if the words were removed. A press at the back of a plant. A handwritten scorecard with "night shift" on it. A conference room that looks like a debrief, with five chairs and a closed laptop, not a stage. If you cannot name the picture, you are not ready to art-direct. You are ready to buy a mood.

Use one claim per page, matching the page's job. The homepage picture supports the role. A proof page picture supports the decision. An about-page picture supports the person who will be on the call in week three. Do not reuse the lobby everywhere because it was expensive. Expense is not relevance.

W3C's WCAG 2 overview treats images as part of web content, under a standard whose first principle is that content must be perceivable. A picture that carries the argument has to be described, and it has to be visible with the words, not swapped in late by a carousel. One still image, chosen, beats five images that rotate before anyone can read them.

## What to reject

Reject the handshake, even a well-lit one of your actual partners. The subject is the failure. A hiring manager who has been burned has seen that frame on the firm that sent thirty resumes and called it a shortlist. The picture reassures your team that you look established. It tells the buyer nothing about the seat.

Reject the city avenue, the airport lounge, and the abstract sculpture in a lobby. They are signs of "business" with no role attached. Reject a collage that tries to cover three practices at once. If this site is for one kind of role, one kind of workplace is enough. A second practice can have its own picture on its own page.

Reject celebration shots: champagne, a gong, a group jump. They claim an outcome you often cannot show, and they look like every other services firm. A burned buyer reads celebration as a substitute for the scorecard. Show the work that happens before anyone is hired.

If the team argues for one handshake because a board member likes it, archive the file. The board is not the hiring manager this page has to win. A picture that comforts the partnership and confuses the buyer has already chosen the wrong audience.

Reject pictures of candidates' faces unless you have written permission and a reason that serves the buyer, not your mood. Candidates are not a texture. A wall of smiling professionals is how firms pretend to have a network. If you cannot say what role those people were hired into, do not use the faces.

## A shot list tied to the role

Build the list from the role sentence, not from a photographer's portfolio.

- The workplace the role sits in, photographed as work, not as architecture. A line, a ward desk, a packing bench. Wide enough to understand, close enough to see the job.
- The artifact you actually use. A one-page scorecard. A shortlist rule. An off-limits list with names covered. The object should be readable, or you should not pretend it is.
- The person who runs that search, at a table with the artifact, not against a gray seamless backdrop. Their hands can be in the frame. Their hobby should not be the subject.
- The client's kind of room, if you are allowed. A small office with a production view. Not their logo wall unless the logo is the point, which it rarely is.

Ten frames is plenty for a small site. You do not need a library. You need three that can carry the homepage, the proof, and the about page. Extra frames become a carousel, and a carousel spends the first 10 seconds on motion instead of on the role.

If you fill two role families, shoot both, and do not blend them in one hero. A clinic and a factory in one frame looks like a stock composite. It tells the buyer you will widen the search the way the last firm did.

## How to brief the photographer

Send the role sentence, the list of rejects, and three references that are about subject, not about color grade. Say what must be readable. Say who may be recognized. Say which rooms are off limits because a search is confidential.

Ask for stills, not a brand film, unless you have a real reason and the discipline to show a poster frame that works with the sound off. Autoplay video is how a handshake returns as motion. A still you chose is easier to judge and easier to keep fast.

Stay for the first setups. The wrong frame is usually obvious in the first twenty minutes: the photographer reaches for a handshake because that is what firms buy. Stop it then. Do not discover it in a gallery of eighty images and feel obliged to use one because the day happened.

Pay for the usage you need on the site, and keep the files. A picture you cannot replace when a crop is wrong will bully the layout later. Name the files by subject, not by IMG number, so the next person does not put the lobby back on the homepage out of confusion.

## Alt text and the caption

Write the alt text from what is in the frame, then the point it serves. "A one-page scorecard on a steel table, with the night-shift line circled, beside a homepage that claims plant leadership." If the image fails, that sentence still carries the claim. "Professional team collaboration" carries nothing, and it stuffs a mood into a description.

Do not hide the role keyword in every alt attribute. The picture is not a billboard for a query. A hiring manager using a screen reader should hear the scene, not a slogan.

Captions can be short. Credit the source if it is not yours. If it is yours, the caption can name the constraint the picture proves. "Scorecard from a plant-manager search. We would not add a sixth criterion." That caption is doing work. "Our people, our passion" is not.

Check contrast if you set type over the photograph. WCAG's perceivable principle is failed when the headline disappears into a bright window or a dark suit. If the picture and the words fight, move the words onto a plain ground. Do not dim the picture into mud so the type can sit on it. A muddy hero is still a hero, and it is now illegible.

## When stock is honest

Stock is honest when it shows a workplace you actually recruit into and you say it is a typical setting, not a client. A real factory aisle, chosen because your searches sit in aisles like that, can be fair. Label it as a typical setting if it is not a client site. Do not imply you placed the person in the frame.

Stock is a costume when it is a handshake, a skyline, or a diverse meeting that could illustrate any article about "business." Those pictures are cheap because they are empty. Emptiness is what a burned buyer is trained to see.

If you cannot shoot this quarter, publish fewer pictures. A site with one true artifact and honest empty space is stronger than a site tiled with handshakes. Add the real frames when you have them. Do not fill the grid to make the design look finished.

The frames also have to survive a phone, where the crop will cut whatever you treated as edge detail. Read [how the first screen has to hold the role on a phone](/blog/the-mobile-visit-for-a-recruiting-firm) before you approve a wide photograph that only works on a desktop.

When you want to see pictures that carry a specific offer instead of a mood, look at [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). Judge the frames by what they claim, not by how polished the grade is.
